explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ease into this one. Matthew says He drove out all who were buying and selling there. I chase one runaway sprinkle across my counter and need a whole afternoon to recover, so I'm impressed.

Sitting back to watch would be a much quieter scene, but that's not what Matthew tells us. The text says Jesus drove out all who were buying and selling. He also overturned tables, and nobody overturns tables from a comfy seat.

explanations.answer: He asks them to move aside
explanations.explanation: A polite request would've made this a calmer story. The text says He drove out all who were buying and selling, and He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. Matthew doesn't mention any gentle request.
Those tables did not stay standing, friend. Matthew says Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers. He also overturned the seats of those selling doves.
Right, those tables did not stay put. Matthew says He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. I couldn't knock over a cooling rack without three apologies.
Jesus declares, "It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’…" Prayer is what He says that house is meant to be. Then He says they are making it "a den of robbers."

Trade is what was going on in the courts, since people were buying and selling there. But the word Jesus quotes is not trade. He says, "My house will be called a house of prayer." The Scripture holds the answer, friend.
Rest sounds nice, I'll admit. I'd take a nap right now if the ovens allowed it. But Jesus quotes, "My house will be called a house of prayer." The word is prayer.

Jesus says to them, "But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’…" He sets a house of prayer right beside a den of robbers, and the two pictures couldn't be further apart. That's some serious contrast, baker.
Lions sound dramatic, and I get why it came to mind. But Jesus doesn't say lions here. He says, "But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’…"
Vipers would make for a wild story, wouldn't it? Jesus uses different words. He says, "But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’…" It's a den, and it's robbers.

Yes! Matthew 21:14 says the blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them. The same passage that has Him driving out buyers and sellers has the blind and the lame coming to Him. That's quite a turn in a few verses.
The text says the opposite, friend. The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them. That's right there in Matthew 21:14, plain as a cookie on a cooling rack.

Matthew says the chief priests and scribes were indignant. That's when they saw the wonders Jesus performed and the children shouting in the temple courts. Same sights, and indignant is the word Matthew gives.
Overjoyed would've been a very different scene. The text says they were indignant when they saw the wonders and heard the children. Same sights, no joy.

Grateful isn't the word Matthew gives us. He says the chief priests and scribes were indignant. They saw the wonders Jesus performed, and they heard the children shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David!"

He sure does. When they ask, "Do You hear what these children are saying?" Jesus answers, "Yes." Then He asks them a question of His own about what they've never read. Loud children are hard to miss, and I speak from experience with loud things in my bakery.
Not quite, friend. When they ask, "Do You hear what these children are saying?" Jesus answers, "Yes." Then He goes straight on to ask them whether they've never read something.
Jesus says, "…'From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.'" The word is praise. He names children and infants as the mouths it comes from.
Wisdom is a good word, but it's not the one Jesus uses. He says, "…'From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.'" That's the line He points them back to.

Prophecy isn't the word here, friend. Jesus says, "…'From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.'" The children were shouting, and the word for what comes from their mouths is praise.
Matthew says Jesus went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night. He left the leaders and the courts behind. Then in the morning He's heading back to the city.
Jericho isn't the town in this passage. Matthew says He went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night. Good guess, friend.
Capernaum isn't in this scene at all. The text says Jesus went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night. In the morning He's returning to the city, hungry.
Matthew says Jesus found nothing on it except leaves. He was hungry when He went up to it. Leaves were all there was.
Plenty of ripe figs isn't what Matthew says. The text says Jesus found nothing on it except leaves. He was hungry when He went up to it, and leaves were all there was.
Even a few small figs would have been something. But the text says He found nothing on it except leaves. Not a one, friend.
Jesus says, "May you never bear fruit again!" and Matthew says immediately the tree withered. No waiting around for a few weeks. It happened right then.
The tree doesn't stay green. After Jesus speaks, Matthew says immediately the tree withered. It went from leaves to withered in no time, baker.
No fresh figs show up here. Jesus says, "May you never bear fruit again!" and the tree withered immediately. It's the opposite of fruit.
That's not what the disciples ask. They marvel and ask, "How did the fig tree wither so quickly?" Their question is about the speed, not about the figs.
Right, that's not their question. The disciples marvel and ask, "How did the fig tree wither so quickly?" They want to know how it happened so fast. That's all they ask.
Jesus says, "if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree…" (Matthew 21:21). Faith and no doubt go together there. Doubt is the word.
Rushing is a fine thing to avoid, trust me. I've pulled a batch out early more than once. But Jesus says, "if you have faith and do not doubt…" and that's the word in the verse.
Wandering isn't in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree…" The word He uses is doubt.

Jesus says, "…even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen." A mountain is a whole lot bigger than a fig tree. He's the one who said it, so that's the picture we get.
The temple is in this passage, but it's not what Jesus names here. He says, "…even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen." The word is mountain.
City walls aren't in the verse. Jesus says, "…even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen." It's a mountain, baker.
Jesus says, "If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer." That's how He ends His answer to the disciples. A promise about prayer, right at the close.

Jesus really does say it. He says, "If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer." That's a promise about believing and praying, given in answer to the disciples' question about the fig tree.
